newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retailers hope for buoyant Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Australian retailers hope for buoyant Christmas.

text.p: Australian retailers, battered by stiff competition and weak consumer confidence, are pinning their hopes on Christmas sales following a recent cut in official interest rates.
"There's no doubt that this Christmas period will be crucial, and not just for us," Dick Warburton, chairman of upmarket retailer David Jones Ltd, said on Tuesday.
"This six-week period coming up is really the make-or-break of the financial year. It's like living on a volcano," he said.
Large department stores would normally earn about a third of annual sales in the December quarter, with the bulk in the lead-up to Christmas, according to industry analysts.
"Obviously they have all got their fingers crossed and are feeling a bit nervous from the way they are talking about their profit trends," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
Another said the outlook did not appear particularly bright.
"The last interest rate cut may have come a little bit too late," he said.

Hopes for a pick-up in sales have been boosted by the half-point cut in official interest rates on November 6 to 6.50 percent, and an 8.3-percent surge in the November Westpac index of consumer confidence.
Warburton described the jump in consumer confidence as encouraging, but told the David Jones annual meeting it was still too early to assess the likely trend of Christmas sales.
Across town, shareholders in Australia's largest retailer, Coles Myer Ltd, were told the rate cut should help confidence but the company did not expect a big lift in sales before mid-1997.
"We are adopting a cautious approach to Christmas, and are conservative in our approach to a quite difficult market," Coles Myer chairman Nobby Clark told the meeting.
However, the company expected some bottom line improvement provided the Christmas trading period was "reasonable", he said.
Woolworths Ltd, meanwhile, told shareholders at its annual general meeting in Sydney last Thursday that its earnings to June 1997 would depend on the Christmas period.
Woolworth's, Australia's second largest retailer and its biggest supermarket operator, plans to launch its advertising and marketing campaign for Christmas early in December.
"A recent consumer confidence survey showed an improvement and we hope this will be reflected in sales this Christmas," Woolworths managing director Reg Clairs told reporters.
